passage:
Sharmila, it's Swati. You asked how I actually decided, so here it is. I took three countries and five things I care about. Family distance mattered most to me, so I gave it a weight of five. Work culture and the visa route each got four. Salary and living cost got three.
Then I scored each country out of ten. Germany came to 112, Singapore 115, Canada 107.
Look at those numbers. They're too close to be a verdict. My scores were guesses, and one different guess changes the order. So I didn't pick Singapore because it won.
What the numbers showed me was why Singapore came first: the flight home is short. That was the thing I hadn't said out loud before.

qa.q: What weight did Swati give to family distance?
qa.a: Swati gave family distance a weight of five.

qa.q: How did Swati feel about the totals being so close?
qa.a: Swati felt cautious and honest about them, saying the scores were guesses and too close to be a verdict.

qa.q: What could Swati do next to test the ranking?
qa.a: Swati could change a few scores and weights to see whether the order shifts, and talk to people living in those countries.

qa.q: How might Sharmila have felt hearing about the decision?
qa.a: Sharmila probably felt curious and appreciated Swati's honest account, since Swati said the numbers were not the verdict.

grounding: The monologue shows a person scoring three countries on salary, visa route, living cost, family distance and work culture with weights, and noting that the scores are approximate.

passage: I'm Uma, and I sit opposite Dhruv at work. For two weeks his second monitor has shown the same spreadsheet: Canada, Germany and Australia down the side, and five columns across: pay, cost of living, visa path, distance from family, work culture. Each column had a small number above it. He told me those were weights. 'Distance from family is 30 percent, because Ma lives alone. Pay is only 15.' He scored each country from one to five and let the sheet multiply. Germany came top by a hair, 3.6 against Canada's 3.5. What struck me was the note he'd typed in red under the totals: 'These are guesses. A 0.1 gap means nothing.' He didn't book anything that day. He said he'd talk to people in both places first. I can't tell if he was relieved or more confused.

qa.q: What weight did Dhruv give to family distance?
What does the red note suggest about Dhruv's attitude?
qa.a: It suggests he is cautious and a little unsure, careful not to let a tiny gap between guessed scores feel like certainty.

qa.q: What else could Dhruv do, given that the totals are so close?
qa.a: He could test the scores that matter most, such as family distance, by talking to Ma and to people living in Germany and Canada.

qa.q: How might Dhruv's mother be affected by the way he weighs the choice?
qa.a: Giving family distance the biggest weight means Ma's situation shapes the decision, which could reassure her.

grounding: It shows a colleague watching someone score three countries on weighted criteria, compare totals and note that the scores are only approximate.

passage:
Saturday. Vishal opens a blank sheet. Three countries across the top: the Netherlands, Ireland, the UAE. Down the side: pay, visa path, cost of living, distance from family, work culture. His friend Madhav asks, 'Aren't they all equal?' 'Not to me,' Vishal says, and gives the visa path 30 percent, because his last application was rejected.
Tuesday. He fills in scores from one to five, using official pages and two friends' replies. Ireland: 3.9. The Netherlands: 3.7. The UAE: 3.4. Under the totals he writes: 'rough scores, could swing'.
The next Sunday. Madhav finds him lowering Ireland's living-cost score after reading about rents. The total drops to 3.6. Vishal just shrugs. 'That's why I wrote rough. Now the Netherlands and Ireland are close, so I'll look at the jobs themselves.'

qa.q: What score did Ireland get on Tuesday?
How does Vishal feel when Ireland's total drops?
qa.a: He seems calm and unbothered, having expected the scores to be rough, so the drop doesn't upset him.

qa.q: What would you advise Vishal now that two countries are close?
qa.a: Compare real job offers and talk to people working in both places, since the matrix has narrowed the list but can't choose for him.

qa.q: How does the matrix look to Madhav?
qa.a: Madhav first thought the factors were equal, but watching Vishal adjust scores he sees a careful, personal method.

grounding: It shows a young man scoring three countries on weighted personal priorities and comparing totals while treating the scores as approximate.
